name: KY-022 infrared receiver module
description: 38 kHz infrared remote-control receiver module with a 1838-series (VS1838B) receiver: it demodulates the IR carrier and outputs the remote's pulse train on S, idling high and going low while IR is received; a red LED flickers with the signal. Decodes NEC remotes such as the kit's car-MP3 remote. Runs on 3.3-5 V. Sold as: Keyes / Joy-IT KY-022 infrared receiver module (black 3-pin sensor-kit board, also sold as HW-490, with 1838 receiver and indicator LED; header S, + (middle), -).
eli5: An invisible-light ear for TV remotes. When you press a button on the remote, it hears the flashes and passes the button's code to your board.

pins.name: S
pins.description: Signal (pin 1): demodulated output, idles high, low while 38 kHz IR is received (active low). Idles at the module supply voltage.
Middle pin (often unlabelled): supply, 3.3-5 V. Use 3V3 with an ESP32 or Pico so S never exceeds 3.3 V.

buildNotes: Header order as printed: S, + (middle), -. Some clones swap S and -; the middle pin is always the supply.
Power the module from 3V3 on an ESP32 or Pico: S idles at the supply voltage, so a 5 V supply puts 5 V on the GPIO.
S is active low: 9 ms low leader, 4.5 ms high, then 32 NEC bits (562.5 us mark, 562.5 us space = 0, 1687.5 us = 1, LSB first).
Decode with an edge interrupt (ir_rx.py, Peter Hinch's micropython_ir). Use NEC_16 for remotes with a 16-bit address.
Keep it out of direct sunlight and away from fluorescent lamps, which add noise.

driver.code:
# peterhinch/micropython_ir (MIT): ir_rx/__init__.py and ir_rx/nec.py merged into one module, otherwise unchanged.
# Source: https://github.com/peterhinch/micropython_ir
# ir_rx __init__.py Decoder for IR remote control using synchronous code
# IR_RX abstract base class for IR receivers.

# Author: Peter Hinch
# Copyright Peter Hinch 2020-2024 Released under the MIT license

# Thanks are due to @Pax-IT for diagnosing a problem with ESP32C3.

from machine import Timer, Pin
from array import array
from utime import ticks_us

# from micropython import alloc_emergency_exception_buf
# alloc_emergency_exception_buf(100)


# On 1st edge start a block timer. While the timer is running, record the time
# of each edge. When the timer times out decode the data. Duration must exceed
# the worst case block transmission time, but be less than the interval between
# a block start and a repeat code start (~108ms depending on protocol)


class IR_RX:
    Timer_id = -1  # Software timer but enable override
    # Result/error codes
    # Repeat button code
    REPEAT = -1
    # Error codes
    BADSTART = -2
    BADBLOCK = -3
    BADREP = -4
    OVERRUN = -5
    BADDATA = -6
    BADADDR = -7

    def __init__(self, pin, nedges, tblock, callback, *args):  # Optional args for callback
        self._pin = pin
        self._nedges = nedges
        self._tblock = tblock
        self.callback = callback
        self.args = args
        self._errf = lambda _: None
        self.verbose = False

        self._times = array("i", (0 for _ in range(nedges + 1)))  # +1 for overrun
        pin.irq(handler=self._cb_pin, trigger=(Pin.IRQ_FALLING | Pin.IRQ_RISING))
        self.edge = 0
        self.tim = Timer(self.Timer_id)  # Defaul is sofware timer
        self.cb = self.decode

    # Pin interrupt. Save time of each edge for later decode.
    def _cb_pin(self, line):
        t = ticks_us()
        # On overrun ignore pulses until software timer times out
        if self.edge <= self._nedges:  # Allow 1 extra pulse to record overrun
            if not self.edge:  # First edge received
                self.tim.init(period=self._tblock, mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, callback=self.cb)
            self._times[self.edge] = t
            self.edge += 1

    def do_callback(self, cmd, addr, ext, thresh=0):
        self.edge = 0
        if cmd >= thresh:
            self.callback(cmd, addr, ext, *self.args)
        else:
            self._errf(cmd)

    def error_function(self, func):
        self._errf = func

    def close(self):
        self._pin.irq(handler=None)
        self.tim.deinit()


# nec.py Decoder for IR remote control using synchronous code
# Supports NEC and Samsung protocols.
# With thanks to J.E. Tannenbaum for information re Samsung protocol

# For a remote using NEC see https://www.adafruit.com/products/389

# Author: Peter Hinch
# Copyright Peter Hinch 2020-2022 Released under the MIT license

from utime import ticks_us, ticks_diff

class NEC_ABC(IR_RX):
    def __init__(self, pin, extended, samsung, callback, *args):
        # Block lasts <= 80ms (extended mode) and has 68 edges
        super().__init__(pin, 68, 80, callback, *args)
        self._extended = extended
        self._addr = 0
        self._leader = 2500 if samsung else 4000  # 4.5ms for Samsung else 9ms

    def decode(self, _):
        try:
            if self.edge > 68:
                raise RuntimeError(self.OVERRUN)
            width = ticks_diff(self._times[1], self._times[0])
            if width < self._leader:  # 9ms leading mark for all valid data
                raise RuntimeError(self.BADSTART)
            width = ticks_diff(self._times[2], self._times[1])
            if width > 3000:  # 4.5ms space for normal data
                if self.edge < 68:  # Haven't received the correct number of edges
                    raise RuntimeError(self.BADBLOCK)
                # Time spaces only (marks are always 562.5µs)
                # Space is 1.6875ms (1) or 562.5µs (0)
                # Skip last bit which is always 1
                val = 0
                for edge in range(3, 68 - 2, 2):
                    val >>= 1
                    if ticks_diff(self._times[edge + 1], self._times[edge]) > 1120:
                        val |= 0x80000000
            elif width > 1700: # 2.5ms space for a repeat code. Should have exactly 4 edges.
                raise RuntimeError(self.REPEAT if self.edge == 4 else self.BADREP)  # Treat REPEAT as error.
            else:
                raise RuntimeError(self.BADSTART)
            addr = val & 0xff  # 8 bit addr
            cmd = (val >> 16) & 0xff
            if cmd != (val >> 24) ^ 0xff:
                raise RuntimeError(self.BADDATA)
            if addr != ((val >> 8) ^ 0xff) & 0xff:  # 8 bit addr doesn't match check
                if not self._extended:
                    raise RuntimeError(self.BADADDR)
                addr |= val & 0xff00  # pass assumed 16 bit address to callback
            self._addr = addr
        except RuntimeError as e:
            cmd = e.args[0]
            addr = self._addr if cmd == self.REPEAT else 0  # REPEAT uses last address
        # Set up for new data burst and run user callback
        self.do_callback(cmd, addr, 0, self.REPEAT)

class NEC_8(NEC_ABC):
    def __init__(self, pin, callback, *args):
        super().__init__(pin, False, False, callback, *args)

class NEC_16(NEC_ABC):
    def __init__(self, pin, callback, *args):
        super().__init__(pin, True, False, callback, *args)

class SAMSUNG(NEC_ABC):
    def __init__(self, pin, callback, *args):
        super().__init__(pin, True, True, callback, *args)

# KY-022 infrared receiver module

## Overview
The **KY-022** (also sold as **HW-490**) is the black 3-pin sensor-kit board carrying a **1838-series 38 kHz IR receiver** (VS1838B / TL1838), a 1 kΩ resistor and a red LED that flickers while a signal is received.
- The receiver detects, amplifies, filters and **demodulates** the 38 kHz carrier from an IR remote; S outputs the envelope as a logic signal.
- S **idles high and goes low while IR carrier is received** (active low).
- Range about 18 m, ±45° acceptance angle; supply 3.3–5 V (chip 2.7–5.5 V), 0.4–1.5 mA quiescent.
- The cheap kit remotes (the 17/21-key "car MP3" remotes) use the **NEC** protocol.

## Pinout (3-pin header, as printed on the board)
| Pin | Name | Function |
|-----|------|----------|
| 1 | S | Demodulated signal output, active low |
| 2 | + (middle, often unlabelled) | Supply, 3.3–5 V |
| 3 | - | Ground |

Some clones swap the outer S and - pins; the middle pin is always the supply. Wire by the labels printed on your board.

## Electrical limits
- Supply 2.7–5.5 V (VS1838B datasheet), 6.0 V absolute maximum; the module is specified for 3.3–5 V.
- Output low ≤ 0.4 V; output high ≈ supply (≥ 4.5 V at 5 V). **Powered from 5 V, S idles at 5 V**: with an ESP32 or Pico power the module from 3V3.
- Current 0.4–1.5 mA idle plus about 2 mA in the LED while S is low.

## Interface details
NEC frame as seen on S (low = carrier present):
- 9 ms low (leader mark), 4.5 ms high (space)
- 32 bits, LSB first: address, ~address, command, ~command. Each bit is a 562.5 µs mark followed by a 562.5 µs space (0) or 1687.5 µs space (1)
- A final 562.5 µs mark. While the button is held, a repeat code (9 ms mark, 2.25 ms space, 562.5 µs mark) every 108 ms
- Extended NEC sends a 16-bit address in place of address/~address (use `NEC_16`)

The driver (Peter Hinch's `micropython_ir`, MIT) timestamps every edge in a pin interrupt, then decodes the block 80 ms after the first edge.

## Wiring
| Module | ESP32 | Raspberry Pi Pico | Raspberry Pi 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| S | GPIO15 | GP16 | GPIO17 (pin 11) |
| + | 3V3 | 3V3(OUT) (pin 36) | 3V3 (pin 1) |
| - | GND | GND | GND |

## Using the driver
```python
from machine import Pin
from ir_rx import NEC_8
import time

def cb(cmd, addr, ctrl):
    if cmd == NEC_8.REPEAT:
        print('repeat')
    elif cmd >= 0:
        print('addr %02x cmd %02x' % (addr, cmd))

ir = NEC_8(Pin(15, Pin.IN), cb)
while True:
    time.sleep_ms(100)
```
`NEC_8` checks the 8-bit address and its inverse; use `NEC_16` for remotes with a 16-bit (extended) address. Negative codes are errors (BADSTART, BADBLOCK, BADDATA, BADADDR...); `ir.error_function(print)` shows them.

## Gotchas
- **No output at all** with correct code: the S and - pins may be swapped on your clone. Check the labels.
- Keep the receiver out of direct sunlight and away from fluorescent/LED lamps; they cause noise bursts.
- The callback runs in a (soft) timer context: keep it short, set a flag and act in the main loop.
- On some ESP32 firmware a software timer `Timer(-1)` is not available: set `IR_RX.Timer_id = 0` (a hardware timer) before creating the decoder.
- The receiver only works with 38 kHz carriers (most consumer remotes). 36/40 kHz remotes give shorter range.
- Long button holds send repeat codes, not the command again: remember the last command if you need auto-repeat.

## Datasheet
https://www.elecrow.com/download/Infrared%20receiver%20vs1838b.pdf
